title: Stoke Rochford Hall Lancaster Memorial

crew.name: Norman William Guy
crew.bio: Son of Albert Joseph and Elizabeth Hearder Guy. Had only 60 flying hours at the time of the crash.

crew.name: Richard Knut Ourom
crew.bio: Son of Ivan and Ida Ourom. His nephew Anders Ourom later spoke at the 2006 dedication ceremony at Stoke Rochford Hall.

crew.name: John Donald Travis
crew.bio: Son of Frederick Joseph and Mary Josephine Travis. His class ring from St Malachy's High School was found among Cline's personal effects and traced back to his family after eleven months of research. His sister Alleyne Murphy later visited the memorial and crash site.

crew.name: Donald Roger Wilson
crew.bio: Son of Lloyd Rogerson Wilson and Marjorie Anna Wilson.

crew.name: Henry William Jones
crew.bio: Son of Henry and Ciselia Bessie Jones. The only non-Canadian crew member, serving with the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve.

crew.name: Verle Edmund Cline
crew.bio: Son of James Edmond and Audrea Loraine Cline. Born in Edmonton, raised in California. Canadian by birth but grew up pledging allegiance to the American flag. Enlisted in the USAF after Pearl Harbor but could not deploy to Europe as a foreign national, so he moved to Canada and joined the RCAF. Known as 'Hap' — short for Happy. His RCAF identity bracelet, inscribed 'Love Marge' by his fiancée Marge Hill, was found at the crash site in 2002 and returned to his sister Vesper Merrit.

crew.name: James Roy Williams
crew.bio: Son of Roy James Williams and Dorothy Belle Williams.

crew_summary: 7 crew — 7 killed (6 RCAF, 1 RAF VR). Pilot Flt Lt Norman William Guy, age 24. All six Canadians buried at Brookwood Military Cemetery; Sgt Jones at Romford Cemetery, Essex.

narrative: Seven men were aboard — six RCAF, one RAF VR. The war in Europe was days from ending. At 03:14 hrs on 28 April, the aircraft lost control and dived into the grounds of Stoke Rochford Hall. The Board of Enquiry cited icing in cumulonimbus cloud and possible instrument failure; the pitot head had likely iced up. Radio contact had been lost, and rocket flares fired to attract attention went unacknowledged. Two eyewitnesses, neither interviewed at the time, independently reported fire before impact — one saw an engine ablaze over Colsterworth, the other watched the aircraft descending with fire in the wing toward Stoke Rochford Hall. A lightning strike is a plausible cause of both the fire and the loss of radio communications. The BOE was critical of the pilot's airmanship, though Flt Lt Guy had only 60 flying hours. Weather was almost certainly the primary factor. All seven crew were killed.
community_connection: The story of this memorial began in Stoke Rochford Hall's gardens, when Head Gardener Clive Robinson found live ammunition while working the grounds. .303 calibre bullets from the 1940s, large pieces of aluminium, and signs of fire — the area had been a wartime parachute training ground, but this was something else. Local wartime crash records had been destroyed in 1955, and local papers had never reported aircraft accidents for fear of affecting morale. An extensive search of archives and newspapers led nowhere. The breakthrough came from Canada. On 6 December 2002, a suspicious parcel arrived at 8th Canadian Wing Headquarters in Trenton, Ontario. Bearing UK stamps but no return address, it was treated as a potential threat — an Explosive Ordnance Disposal team was flown in from London, Ontario, and a robot X-rayed the package. Inside was an RCAF identity bracelet engraved with 'V. Cline' and service number R279050. Below, in script: 'Love Marge'. An anonymous note read: 'This article was discovered at Stoke Rochford on an RCAF crash site dating from the 45 era. I believe that you are best placed to know appropriate actions for such an object.' The bracelet unlocked everything. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission confirmed that Sergeant Verle Edmond Cline, aged 21, was buried at Brookwood Military Cemetery. From there, the RAF Air Historical Branch at Hendon identified the aircraft, the squadron, and all seven crew. Verle Cline's own story is remarkable. Born Canadian in Edmonton, he grew up in Willows, California, pledging allegiance to the American flag. After Pearl Harbor he enlisted in the US Air Force, but as a Canadian citizen he could not deploy to Europe with his unit. Undaunted, he moved back to Canada and joined the RCAF as an air gunner. While training in Montreal he met 19-year-old Marge Hill at a tobogganing club on Mount Royal. They fell in love and planned to marry after the war. She gave him the bracelet shortly before he left for Europe. His diary for September 1944 reads 'Engaged to Marge'; for October, simply 'Waiting to see Marge.' Marge learned the full story of his death only when the bracelet surfaced — sixty years later. Cline's sister Vesper Merrit, traced to Soquel, California, was presented with the bracelet. 'I'm going to wear it,' she said. 'This is closure.' A second discovery followed. Marge had kept it for sixty years. The Canadian authorities traced the motto to St Malachy's High School in Saint John, New Brunswick, identifying the true owner: Flying Officer John Donald Travis, the wireless operator. The ring had likely ended up in Cline's locker by accident as the crew prepared for the flight. Simultaneously, Travis's sister Alleyne Murphy had been searching the internet for information about her brother. She found his name on the Stoke Rochford memorial page and contacted David Frampton, learning for the first time how John had died. Her brother's ring was returned to her at a ceremony at RCAF Trenton on the 65th anniversary of the crash. In October 2010, Alleyne travelled from Nova Scotia to visit her brother's grave and the crash site. The Grantham Branch of the Royal Air Forces Association organised a ceremony in her honour. The research behind this memorial was carried out by former Warrant Officer Class One David Frampton, whose five-part account is available as a downloadable document on this page.
memorial_details:
Dedicated 19 November 2006 at Stoke Rochford Hall. Over 200 attendees including Canadian relatives, Canadian High Commission, senior RAF officers, and 22 Standards of the RAFA, Royal British Legion, and Ex-Service Associations. Plaque cast from salvaged aircraft metal by Cpl Ian Harrison RAF, RAF Cottesmore. Canadian Maple tree (Acer Rubrum) donated by Stoke Rochford Management Ltd. Registered on the UK Inventory of War Memorials (Imperial War Museum).

Moved by the memorial, she funded the planting of a dwarf quince beneath the plaque — chosen because it flowers at the end of April, the anniversary of the crash.
